analysis.one_liner: Caps federal student aid to for-profit colleges by requiring they enroll at least 15% non-federal-paying students.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action after being referred to the Senate HELP Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the share of revenue that for-profit colleges must draw from non-federal sources from 10% to 15%, counting GI Bill and military tuition benefits as federal money, restricting how schools can count scholarships and loans as non-federal revenue, and making schools lose federal student aid eligibility immediately after a single violation instead of only after two consecutive years of non-compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges, especially veterans and military service members whose GI Bill and tuition assistance benefits would count as federal student aid in the compliance test, gain protection from schools that rely almost entirely on federal dollars rather than student outcomes. Taxpayers gain by reducing federal student aid and loan dollars flowing to for-profit schools that historically leave taxpayers holding the bag for defaulted loans.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the non-federal revenue requirement for proprietary colleges from 10% to 15%, reducing the incentive for schools to enroll students solely to capture federal aid.

Counts GI Bill benefits and military tuition assistance as federal funds for the first time, closing a loophole that let for-profit schools count veteran education benefits toward the non-federal share.
Makes loss of federal aid eligibility immediate after a single year of non-compliance instead of requiring two consecutive years of violation.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies lose some federal revenue and some schools could lose access to federal student aid entirely. Some students at marginal for-profit programs could lose access to those programs if schools close or cut offerings.

drawbacks.text: Students enrolled at for-profit schools that fail the test could see their programs close, forcing them to transfer credits that may not carry over.
The bill only regulates proprietary (for-profit) institutions, leaving other sectors of higher education untouched, so it targets one sector rather than setting a standard for all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects students and taxpayers from a sector with historically high default rates and low completion rates. Costs fall on the for-profit college industry, and the cost to students—disrupted programs—is real but weighed against the risk of taking on debt for a credential that leaves them unable to repay. On balance the benefits likely outweigh the costs for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and died there with no further action before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 31, 2017 and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges kept access to federal student aid and veteran education dollars under the existing 90/10 rule, which they continued to meet in part by counting GI Bill benefits as non-federal revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges kept federal aid access

for.name: Sen. Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republicans supported the bill.

industries.note: For-profit schools rely heavily on federal student aid and veteran benefits for revenue. The bill cuts into that revenue by raising the non-federal share requirement and closing the GI Bill loophole.
